stories.headline: Trump threatens to double tariffs on Mexico if migrant caravans not stopped
stories.note: Trump is using real leverage to make Mexico stop the caravans before they reach the border.
body: President Trump warned Mexico on Thursday morning that he will double U.S. tariffs on the country right away if it fails to halt migrant caravans moving north toward the southern border.

In a Truth Social post, Trump said the people in the caravans "will not be accepted" and that Mexico, Texas officials, Border Patrol and ICE had all been notified. "There will be no leniency!" he wrote.

Trump tied the new caravans to the midterm results, arguing that a perceived Republican loss has encouraged a fresh push of illegal migration. The group, estimated at about 1,500 people mostly from Central America, left Tapachula near the Guatemala border on Tuesday.

The report notes that newly elected Democratic state attorneys general, including Texas AG-elect Nathan Johnson, could drop the defense of tough state border laws like Texas' SB4. Florida AG James Uthmeier pushed back on any talk of amnesty, pointing to record deportations of criminal illegal immigrants in his state.
Why it matters: Trump is showing he will use economic pressure to keep the border closed, drawing a sharp contrast with Democrats who are positioning to roll back enforcement once they take power.

stories.headline: Top House Dem sparks backlash with plan for deported Dreamers that goes beyond bringing them back
stories.note: Democrats' first big immigration idea is already drawing fire as overreach.
body: House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said in a PBS NewsHour interview that he would "certainly" support bringing deported DACA recipients back to the United States, and that people he believes were treated unfairly by the Trump administration should get "remedial assistance."

Jeffries did not say whether that assistance would include money, and his office did not answer Fox News Digital's request for comment. Critics quickly accused him of wanting to pay deported immigrants.

Conservative voices piled on online, with podcaster Benny Johnson saying Democrats "always put foreigners before Americans." Jeffries also called the immigration system broken, vowed not to fund what he called a "violent mass deportation machine," and floated the Dream and Promise Act as a starting point.

DHS has stressed that DACA does not give anyone legal status, and said earlier this year that more than 92% of DACA recipients ICE arrested over most of 2025 had been charged with or convicted of crimes. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said any path to permanent status is up to Congress, while Trump and Mullin have ruled out amnesty.
Why it matters: Before Democrats even take the gavel, their top House leader is handing Republicans a clear message that the new majority will put deported migrants ahead of American taxpayers.

stories.headline: Dems admit uncomfortable election sweep truth as party descends on Denver to shape 2028 without a frontrunner
stories.note: Even after their wins, Democrats admit they have no clear leader heading into 2028.
body: Democratic leaders, strategists and possible 2028 hopefuls are gathering in Denver for a three-day "What's Next" conference hosted by Majority Democrats, a group led by Rep. Jake Auchincloss, to plan the party's direction after its midterm wins.

The speaker list includes Pete Buttigieg, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Sens. Cory Booker, Raphael Warnock and Elissa Slotkin, Sen.-elect James Talarico, Govs. Mikie Sherrill and Abigail Spanberger, Rep. Ro Khanna and David Axelrod.
A senior adviser to the group, longtime strategist Lis Smith, admitted the results were "more a repudiation of Donald Trump than a validation of our party."

The report notes the party still has no clear 2028 frontrunner and must figure out how to unite its progressive and moderate wings while delivering on promises about costs and healthcare, as leaders also pledge to investigate the Trump administration.
Why it matters: Democrats' own strategists concede voters didn't embrace their party so much as vote against Trump, a sign their new majority rests on shaky ground heading into 2028.

stories.headline: At least 9 new Dem members will carry Al Green's mantle and try to impeach President Trump
stories.note: Incoming Democrats are already signaling impeachment, handing the GOP an overreach message.
body: At least nine incoming progressive House Democrats are expected to back efforts to impeach President Trump, picking up a push led by outgoing Rep. Al Green of Texas, Fox News Digital reported exclusively.

Green, who filed impeachment articles in August, named Reps.-elect Melat Kiros, Dan Koh, Chris Rabb and Angela Gonzales-Torres among those he expects to carry on the effort. "The end is to have the president removed from office," Green said, citing Trump's cryptocurrency dealings.

The activist groups behind the push, the Removal Coalition and the Courage for Democracy Project, admitted it may not succeed, since the Senate would need a two-thirds vote to convict, as in Trump's two earlier impeachments. They also want to impeach War Secretary Pete Hegseth.

The Removal Coalition's founder even called Democrats who prefer hearings over impeachment "spineless," vowing grassroots pressure to bring them along. Trump and Hegseth did not respond to requests for comment.

Why it matters: Before the new Congress is even sworn in, the Democratic base is demanding impeachment, giving Republicans a ready-made argument that the new majority cares more about revenge than results.

stories.headline: Twice-deported United cockpit suspect granted asylum after transgender persecution claim: DHS
stories.note: DHS details how a twice-deported suspect won asylum, fueling the case for tougher immigration rules.
body: DHS confirmed that Rony Alexander Gomez-Alberto, a 34-year-old Honduran accused of trying to storm the cockpit of a United Airlines flight while claiming to have a bomb, had been granted asylum after saying he feared being killed back home because he was transgender.

According to DHS, he was deported after illegal entries in 2011 and 2014, caught again near San Ysidro in 2019, released by ICE in January 2020 on a judge's order, and later granted asylum by an immigration judge.

He was arrested when United Flight 2174 landed in New Orleans on Nov. 9 and is being held without bond on charges including terrorizing and communicating false information of planned arson. ICE has lodged a detainer with the local sheriff.
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the suspect got in because of "a weak asylum system that allowed him to game the system."
Why it matters: The case gives Republicans a vivid example of asylum loopholes just as Democrats prepare to take power and push to loosen enforcement.

stories.headline: Biden ripped for 'totally delusional' claim about debate that preceded his 2024 exit
stories.note: Biden reopens an embarrassing chapter for Democrats with his latest debate claim.
body: Former President Joe Biden told People Magazine in an interview released Wednesday that his June 2024 debate against Donald Trump was "not very consequential" — even though he quit the race just 24 days later.
Biden said everyone makes mistakes in debates and that he had expected a second debate that never happened.

Republicans pounced online. Former Trump campaign aide Steve Cortes pointed out the 24-day gap, commentator Steve Guest called Biden "TOTALLY delusional," and former NRSC adviser Matt Whitlock called it the most consequential presidential debate in history.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis also jabbed that it was the most lopsided debate ever. Biden's office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.
Why it matters: Biden's revisionism reopens one of the most damaging episodes in recent Democratic history and the questions about who knew what about his condition.

stories.headline: Ilhan Omar appears clueless on basis for federal probes: 'You probably have more details on that'
stories.note: Omar's shaky answer keeps the spotlight on the federal probes surrounding her.
body: Rep. Ilhan Omar told Fox News Digital on Tuesday that federal agencies never told her the grounds for the investigations into her, and said she wasn't even sure how many probes there are. "You probably have more details on that," she said.

There are two known federal probes: a DHS look at whether her immigration paperwork was filled out fraudulently, and a review of discrepancies in her financial disclosures that D.C. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro has publicly confirmed.

The investigations gained attention after Homeland Security Investigations agents raided her Washington residence on Oct. 12, reportedly seizing her phone, passport and computer and obtaining a DNA sample. Omar said she has gotten most of the items back.

A federal court filing has identified her as "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi," matching the name of her ex-husband, who reports allege is her brother. Omar met with her lawyers for about two hours on Tuesday, and her team did not respond to a request for comment.
Why it matters: Omar's vague answers keep the spotlight on serious federal questions surrounding one of the left's most prominent members as she returns to Capitol Hill.
